# Using ISLA {#sec-using}

**ISLA ships as one class with one reference configuration, trained and
evaluated by the unified external-aerodynamics recipe. This chapter is the
operating manual.** It tells you which configuration to run and what the
few remaining arguments are for. It states what the model needs from your
data (a dictionary of boundary meshes, a point cloud to predict at, and the
problem's named fields of declared rank), how to read the prediction off
the returned mesh, and the commands that train and evaluate it. It tells
you how to set the learning rate when you change the width or depth, how to
use the inference sampler that removes most of the draw noise at a fixed
cell budget, how to load a checkpoint, and what a step costs. Everything
here is about ISLA unless an option is named. The reasons behind each
recommendation are in @sec-isla and the evidence chapters, cited where they
apply.

```{python}
#| label: setup-using
#| include: false
import sys; sys.path.insert(0, ".")
from palette import *
import json
from pathlib import Path
RES = Path("..") / "results"
```

## Which configuration {#sec-using-config}

**Run ISLA as the class ships it. The constructor takes the field
declarations and the task; everything else is a default.** A surface model
that predicts pressure and wall shear stress under one far-field direction
is

```python
from physicsnemo.experimental.models import ISLA
model = ISLA(outputs={"pressure": {"rank": 0}, "wss": {"rank": 1}}, global_inputs={"freestream": {"rank": 1}})
```

and an interior model adds `interior=True`. The defaults are the reference
configuration: 384 wide with 12 layers and 256 slices, cosine routing at a
fixed temperature, the RMS-pairwise-distance length unit, the fused
geometry kernel where it can run, and prediction points that carry a
learned share of the total boundary measure. The recipe's ISLA
configurations (`isla_surface`, `isla_volume`) state the same dimensions and
train at learning rate 5e-4 (the reference selection, @sec-nb-ref-verdict).
This is the one place the book states them, and the width and depth ladders
of @sec-review-frontier are deviations from it. Lanes of the earlier
protocol ran 192 wide at 1e-3 and are labeled so wherever they appear.

**The option policy.** An option is a scaffold under a universalization
test, run always-on across the datasets its rule was not fitted on
(@sec-nb-universal-prereg); it becomes part of the reference configuration
for every dataset or it is deleted, and no option is set per dataset. Every
ratio the book labels "GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA" is the reference
configuration; an option's number is labelled by arm. What remains on the
class is short:

- **the sizes** `hidden`, `n_layers`, `n_slices`, `mlp_ratio`, which set
  capacity and are the axes of the ladders in @sec-capacity;
- **the three cost knobs** `geo_kernel`, `geo_checkpoint` and
  `interior_nn_chunk`, which change how the arithmetic is executed and never
  what is computed (@sec-using-cost);
- **the one option in flight**, `slice_prototypes`: `"static"` (the
  default) or `"centered"`, sample-conditioned prototypes under their
  universalization test (@sec-nb-proto-cond-2-prereg);
- **the spatial dimension** `dim`, 3 by default and 2 for a planar
  problem, which is not an option in the policy's sense but a statement
  about the data (@sec-arch-switches).

Every checkpoint stores its constructor arguments, so a saved model loads
in the configuration that trained it (@sec-using-checkpoint).

::: {.callout-note title="The prediction at a point depends on the request"}
An interior prediction is a function of the whole set of prediction points,
because those points are interacting tokens (@sec-arch-modes). Deploy an
interior model at its training point count and state that count with every
interior number (@sec-using-checkpoint, @sec-interior-companion). A decode
whose answer at a point is independent of the request was built, priced at
several times the interacting decode's error, and removed from the class
(@sec-arch-passive-decoder).
:::

## What the model needs from your data {#sec-using-inputs}

**ISLA takes the boundary as named meshes, the prediction points as a point
cloud, and the problem's data as named fields of declared rank; it returns
a point cloud with the outputs in its point data. The two inputs that are
easy to get wrong are the effective measures, which must sum to the
boundary's measure, and the global directions, which must be directions.**
The forward call is keyword-only and takes three things:

- `boundary_meshes`: a mapping from a name (one entry per boundary
  condition or part) to a `Mesh` of codimension one, a surface in three
  dimensions or a polyline in two. Its cells are the tokens: the cell
  centroid is the position, the cell normal the outward normal, and the
  cell's effective measure (`cell_data["_effective_measure"]`, when present,
  else the geometric measure) the area it stands for. Every declared
  `boundary_inputs` field is read from each mesh's `cell_data` by name.
- `prediction_points`: for the interior task, a point-cloud `Mesh` whose
  `points` are the prediction points and whose `point_data` carries the
  declared `query_inputs`, or a bare `(N, dim)` tensor when none are
  declared. Omitted on a surface task, where the outputs come back at the
  boundary cells.
- `global_data`: a TensorDict or mapping with the declared `global_inputs`
  as leaves: a `(dim,)` vector for a rank-1 field, a scalar for a rank-0
  field. Extra leaves are ignored; a missing one is an error.

The running example shows the whole exchange on the Joukowski airfoil in
two dimensions, with a model too small to predict anything, so the shapes
can be read:

```{python}
#| label: using-forward-demo
#| echo: true
import warnings; warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
import torch
from physicsnemo.mesh import Mesh
from physicsnemo.experimental.models import ISLA

J = joukowski(n_cells=80)                                                   # the book's running example
verts = torch.as_tensor(J["xy"], dtype=torch.float32)                        # (81, 2) polyline vertices, closed
cells = torch.stack([torch.arange(80), torch.arange(1, 81)], dim=1)          # (80, 2) segments; a cell's normal follows its vertex order
airfoil = Mesh(points=verts, cells=cells)                                    # Mesh[1, 2]: a polyline in the plane
outward = ((airfoil.cell_centroids - verts.mean(0)) * airfoil.cell_normals).sum(-1)
if outward.mean() < 0:                                                       # the model reads the cell normals as outward: orient the cells so they are
    airfoil = Mesh(points=verts, cells=cells.flip(1))
    outward = -outward
assert outward.mean() > 0

surface = ISLA(outputs={"cp": {"rank": 0}, "tau": {"rank": 1}}, global_inputs={"freestream": {"rank": 1}}, hidden=32, n_layers=2, n_slices=8, dim=2).eval()
with torch.no_grad():
    out = surface(boundary_meshes={"airfoil": airfoil}, global_data={"freestream": torch.tensor([1.0, 0.1])})
print("surface task:", {k: tuple(v.shape) for k, v in out.point_data.items()}, "at", tuple(out.points.shape), "boundary cells")

interior = ISLA(outputs={"cp": {"rank": 0}}, global_inputs={"freestream": {"rank": 1}}, interior=True, hidden=32, n_layers=2, n_slices=8, dim=2).eval()
grid = torch.stack(torch.meshgrid(torch.linspace(-1.5, 2.5, 40), torch.linspace(-1.5, 1.5, 30), indexing="ij"), -1).reshape(-1, 2)
with torch.no_grad():
    field = interior(boundary_meshes={"airfoil": airfoil}, prediction_points=grid, global_data={"freestream": torch.tensor([1.0, 0.1])})
print("interior task:", tuple(field.point_data["cp"].shape), "predictions at", tuple(field.points.shape), "points")
```

The output is a point-cloud `Mesh`. On the surface task its `points` are
the boundary token positions in token order (the meshes concatenated in
sorted key order); on the interior task they are the prediction points.
Its `point_data` holds one leaf per declared output at its natural shape:
`(N,)` at rank 0, `(N, dim)` at rank 1, `(N, dim, dim)` at rank 2. Its
`global_data` is the selected `global_data` passed through.

Four of the inputs need a word.

- **The effective measures must sum to the boundary's measure.** When the
  recipe keeps $n$ of $N$ cells, each kept cell carries the Horvitz–Thompson
  weight: its area times $N/n$, stored as the mesh's `_effective_measure`
  cell field. The measures then stand for the full surface at any
  `sampling_resolution`, and the routing's quadrature sums read the surface
  area rather than the retained fraction of it. The length unit normalizes
  the measures and is indifferent to the factor, but the quadrature sums
  are not. A boundary passed whole, like the airfoil above, needs no such
  field: the geometric measure of each cell is the measure. Measures carry
  their represented dimension and follow geometric scaling: on a
  two-dimensional problem such as AirfRANS the measure is the segment
  length.
- **A rank-1 global input is a direction.** The problem's global
  directions (the rank-1 entries of `global_inputs`) enter as unit vectors.
  The model normalizes each again internally and discards its magnitude.
  For external aerodynamics the recipe's `ComputeFreestreamDirection`
  writes the direction from the solver's velocity. This is also the
  fair-comparison rule for every architecture in the book
  (@sec-unit-direction-rule).
- **A global direction must be a datum of the problem.** The inlet
  direction, a load direction, a body-force direction (gravity) are
  admissible. The axes of the dataset's coordinate frame are not: they
  describe how the cases were posed, not the PDE, and a solver never takes
  them (@sec-pose-prior). Ground planes and symmetry planes are real
  boundaries and belong among the boundary meshes, not in `global_inputs`.
- **A magnitude that matters is a rank-0 global input.** Declare it
  (`u_inf: {rank: 0}`) and pass it under its name; a parameter vector is several
  rank-0 names, one per parameter. No fixed power of a far-field speed is a
  physical law for every output (a pressure coefficient is degree zero, a
  dimensional pressure degree two), so the model learns the dependence like
  any other parameter. The AirfRANS configuration passes the inlet speed
  this way.

For the interior task the model needs the prediction points and nothing
else about them. It computes each point's direction and signed distance to
the wall from the boundary sample (the nearest boundary cell,
@sec-arch-modes). No signed-distance field has to be stored, sampled or
declared. The distance is to the sampled boundary, not the full mesh. A
dataset that carries a full-mesh signed-distance field can pass it, and its
gradient, as declared `query_inputs` (`sdf: {rank: 0}`, `sdf_gradient: {rank: 1}`) in the
prediction mesh's `point_data`; they enter like any other PDE datum, and
what they buy over the built-in geometry is measured in
@sec-nb-internal-geometry-verdict.

**The recipe's contract.** In the recipe a model configuration declares
`input_type: mesh` and `output_type: mesh`. Under the first, the datapipe's
`Mesh` objects and per-case tensors pass to `forward` as they are, one case
per step with no batch axis, through a `forward_kwargs` mapping whose keys
are the three argument names above and whose values name the datapipe
fields (the boundary meshes under `boundary_meshes`, the sampled interior
point set under `prediction_points`, the case's global tensors under
`global_data`). Under the second, the recipe reads its targets out of the
returned mesh's `point_data` by the same names as the `outputs`
declaration. GLOBE uses the same contract, so the two models are swapped by
changing the model block alone.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Nested field names"}
A dataset that stores its fields in groups (`solution/pressure` on disk,
`solution.pressure` in a config) names its targets with a dot, and the
model's `outputs` declaration uses the same dotted names. A dotted name or a
nested mapping spells a group: every value of `outputs`, `global_inputs`,
`boundary_inputs` and `query_inputs` is a `{rank: ...}` spec or a nested
group of them (a mapping of mappings). So
`outputs: {"solution.pressure": {"rank": 0}, "solution.velocity": {"rank": 1}}` declares two
leaves of one group, and `{"solution": {"pressure": {"rank": 0}, "velocity": {"rank": 1}}}`
declares the same model. The returned mesh's `point_data` is nested the
same way, so `out.point_data["solution", "pressure"]` and
`out.point_data["solution"]["pressure"]` both address the first. The same
dotted names address the fields in the meshes' `cell_data` and
`point_data` and in `global_data`.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Problems other than external aerodynamics"}
The architecture knows only that it was handed named fields of declared
rank. A buoyant flow passes gravity as its one direction. A magnetized flow
passes two. Steady conduction with pinned temperatures passes no direction
and supplies the pinned values as a rank-0 boundary input
(`boundary_inputs: {trace: {rank: 0}}`) on the mesh of the pinned boundary. An
elasticity problem passes its prescribed displacement and traction as
rank-1 boundary inputs (`bc_displacement: {rank: 1}`, `bc_traction: {rank: 1}`); a planar
dataset that stored the components separately stacks them with
`StackScalarFields` in its dataset yaml, and is passed with `dim=2`. It
predicts the stress as a symmetric rank-2 output
(`stress: {rank: 2, symmetric: true}`), and the recipe reads off its
laboratory components for a `symmetric_tensor` target. Each global
direction adds one seed cosine, one relational cosine and two vectors to
the output basis. Each rank-1 boundary input adds its frame cosines and
norm to the seed and one relational cosine per slice
(@sec-isla-inputs-rank). The tests in `test_isla_global_inputs.py`,
`test_isla_inputs.py`, `test_isla_heads.py` and `test_isla_nd.py` cover zero
and two directions, global scalars, rank-1 and rank-2 inputs, every output
rank and parity, and two dimensions. The rank-1-input solids
configurations run the fused geometry kernel in three dimensions; its
limits are in @sec-isla-inputs-rank and the switch in @sec-using-cost.
:::

## Training {#sec-using-train}

**Train at the recipe defaults, 200,000 sampled cells per case for 500
epochs at learning rate 5e-4, with no augmentation. The only setting that
needs thought is the learning rate when you leave width 384.** From the
recipe root:

```bash
# DrivAerML Surface task (sampling_resolution defaults to 200,000 cells per case).
# compile=false is the configuration of the evidence lanes; the compiled path computes the same function faster.
# The ISLA configs pin training.optimizer.lr=5e-4; it is stated here so the protocol is explicit.
python src/train.py model=isla_surface dataset=drivaer_ml_surface \
    training.optimizer.lr=5e-4 compile=false

# DrivAerML Volume task: boundary -> interior, the prediction points as interacting tokens; their direction and
# wall distance are computed inside the model from the boundary sample.
python src/train.py model=isla_volume dataset=drivaer_ml_volume_reference \
    training.optimizer.lr=5e-4 compile=false

# HiLiftAeroML surface (the 200,000-cell default again; 500 epochs, as on the cars)
python src/train.py model=isla_surface dataset=highlift_surface \
    training.optimizer.lr=5e-4 compile=false training.num_epochs=500
```

These commands are the reporting protocol of @sec-protocol. ISLA needs no
rotation augmentation. The contracts make it exact, and a model trained in
the dataset's native frame predicts a body in any pose (@sec-pose).

### The learning rate {#sec-using-lr}

**Use 5e-4 at the reference width 384 and 12 layers. For a wider or deeper
model, start from $10^{-3} \times 192 / \mathrm{hidden} \times 12 /
\mathrm{layers}$ and treat it as a starting rate, not a limit.** The
expression gives $10^{-3}$ at width 192, $5 \times 10^{-4}$ at 384,
$2.5 \times 10^{-4}$ at 768, and $2.5 \times 10^{-4}$ at 384 wide and 24
layers. Every width and depth in the capacity ladders trains cleanly at
this rate, and the ladders of @sec-review-frontier run at it. A model
trained at the rule rate is therefore comparable with the book's lanes.
Under ISLA's cosine routing the logits are bounded, so the routing-collapse
failure that would otherwise set a hard ceiling on the rate is unreachable
(@sec-isla-routing-forms). A higher rate is an experiment, not a hazard.
The recipe's ISLA configurations pin 5e-4 rather than inheriting the
recipe-wide default. The interior standings of @sec-interior are the
reference configuration's at 5e-4. GeoTransolver-volume trains at 1e-3,
its best rate there.

## Evaluation and the inference sampler {#sec-using-sampler}

**Score in float32 at the reporting protocol's 200,000 cells. If the cell
budget is fixed and smaller, draw the cells with the stratified sampler.**
Inference shares the training configuration and reads the checkpoint by run
identifier:

```bash
# sampling_resolution=200000 is the reporting protocol; the infer default is the whole mesh
python src/infer.py model=isla_surface dataset=drivaer_ml_surface \
    run_id=<the trained run_id> infer_split=val sampling_resolution=200000 precision=float32
```

Report in float32. The recipe trains under bf16 autocast, and every number
in this book is a float32 inference on the final-epoch checkpoint
(@sec-metrics). A bf16 inference differs from the float32 one by rounding
of order a percent. Under a rigid motion of the input, its prediction moves
by several percent, where the float32 prediction moves at the level of
float32 roundoff (the residuals are tabulated in @sec-isla-contracts). If
the pose or the sampling-consistency contract is load-bearing, infer in
float32.

**For inference at a fixed cell budget, draw the cells with the stratified
sampler.** Replace the dataset's `SubsampleMesh` stage with the recipe's
`StratifiedSubsampleMesh`:

```yaml
    - _target_: ${dp:StratifiedSubsampleMesh}   # in place of SubsampleMesh
      n_cells: ${sampling_resolution}
```

It keeps the same inclusion law (every cell kept with probability $n/N$,
weight $N/n$), so nothing about the trained model or the quantity it
estimates changes. The kept cells are a *systematic* draw along the Morton
order of the cell centroids: one cell per consecutive run of $N/n$ cells,
with a single random offset. The Morton order sorts cells by interleaved
coordinate bits, a space-filling curve along which consecutive cells are
spatial neighbors. A systematic sample has the same expectation as an
independent draw for every cell-weighted integral and a lower variance for
smooth integrands. The effect is a free improvement for every model and
largest for ISLA, whose slice states are the noisiest estimates
(@sec-deficit-anatomy).

The book keeps the independent draw for its headline comparisons. For a
deployment, use the stratified draw or more cells.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="How many cells"}
Use 200,000 cells. Error is flat above 100,000 (@sec-equal-budget). If the
budget forces fewer cells, use the stratified draw.
:::

## Loading a trained model {#sec-using-checkpoint}

**A checkpoint carries its own constructor arguments, so loading is one
call and the forward call mirrors the recipe mapping.** A saved ISLA is a
PhysicsNeMo module checkpoint and loads with the class's `from_checkpoint`.
No configuration has to be repeated:

```python
from physicsnemo.experimental.models import ISLA
model = ISLA.from_checkpoint("checkpoints/isla_surface.mdlus").eval()
out = model(boundary_meshes={"vehicle": vehicle}, global_data={"freestream": g_hat})
p, tau = out.point_data["pressure"], out.point_data["wss"]  # (N,) and (N, 3), at out.points
```

`vehicle` is a `Mesh` whose cells are the sampled surface, with the
Horvitz–Thompson measures in its `_effective_measure` cell field when the
surface is subsampled. `global_data` maps each declared name to its tensor:
`(3,)` for a direction, a scalar for a rank-0 field. The output is a
point-cloud `Mesh` whose `point_data` is keyed by the declared output names
(a dotted name is a nested leaf), each field with as many trailing axes of
size 3 as its rank. For interior prediction with a model built with
`interior=True`, pass `prediction_points` (a `(Q, 3)` tensor, or a
point-cloud `Mesh` carrying the declared `query_inputs` in its
`point_data`) and read the output at those points. The model derives each
point's direction and signed wall distance from the boundary sample; a
checkpoint that declared a stored signed-distance field among its
`query_inputs` expects it in the prediction mesh's `point_data`, as its
constructor arguments record. Deploy at the training point count (200,000
at the reporting protocol on DrivAerML), because the interacting decode's
prediction at a point depends on the joint request
(@sec-interior-companion).

## Cost {#sec-using-cost}


```{python}
#| label: para-using-cost-lede
#| output: asis
CSW = {r["arm"]: r for r in json.load(open(RES / "cost_sweep_ref_gb300_bf16_2026-09-22.json"))["runs"] if r["tokens"] == 200000 and r["status"] == "ok"}
_med = lambda v: sorted(v)[len(v) // 2]
_isla, _gt, _gt512 = CSW["isla_ref_r1_384x12_cos_fused"], CSW["geotransolver_256"], CSW["geotransolver_512"]
print(f"**At the reporting protocol of 200,000 cells per case, ISLA trains at {_isla['peak_allocated_gib'] / _gt['peak_allocated_gib']:.2f}x "
      f"GeoTransolver-256's peak memory and {_med(_isla['step_ms']) / _med(_gt['step_ms']):.2f}x its step time. GeoTransolver-512, "
      f"the parameter match, costs {_med(_gt512['step_ms']) / _med(_isla['step_ms']):.2f}x ISLA's step time and "
      f"{_gt512['peak_allocated_gib'] / _isla['peak_allocated_gib']:.1f}x its memory.** @tbl-isla-cost reads the three footprints from one "
      "cost sweep on one GB300.")
```
 The step is memory-bound at every stage
but the MLP. The per-slice geometry (separations, invariants, routing
softmaxes) is most of the stored activations. That is why the eager path
rebuilds it in the backward pass instead of storing it (`geo_checkpoint`,
bitwise identical outputs and gradients), and why a fused Triton kernel
exists for the geometry region. `geo_kernel: null` resolves to the kernel
at the first forward pass wherever it can run, and to the eager recompute
region elsewhere (@sec-arch-switches; the conditions are in the list
below). Every path computes the same function (output relative L2 against
the eager reference at most $5.5 \times 10^{-7}$ in bf16,
@sec-nb-geokernel-auto). That footprint is what buys accuracy at scale. On
the DrivAerML Surface task at 435 cars, ISLA reaches GeoTransolver's floor
at less than a third of the memory (@sec-shared-floor).

```{python}
#| label: tbl-isla-cost
#| output: asis
rows = [("ISLA (reference configuration, fused kernel)", "isla_ref_r1_384x12_cos_fused"), ("GeoTransolver-256", "geotransolver_256"), ("GeoTransolver-512 (the parameter match)", "geotransolver_512")]
out = "| architecture | parameters | peak memory per device [GiB] | median step [ms] | ÷ ISLA: parameters | ÷ ISLA: memory | ÷ ISLA: step |\n|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|\n"
i = CSW[rows[0][1]]
for lab, k in rows:
    c = CSW[k]
    out += (f"| {lab} | {c['n_params']/1e6:.1f}M | {c['peak_allocated_gib']:.1f} | {_med(c['step_ms']):.0f} | {c['n_params']/i['n_params']:.2f}x | "
            f"{c['peak_allocated_gib']/i['peak_allocated_gib']:.2f}x | {_med(c['step_ms'])/_med(i['step_ms']):.2f}x |\n")
print(out)
print(": Training cost at the reporting protocol on the DrivAerML Surface task: one case of 200,000 sampled cells per step, bfloat16 autocast, "
      "one GB300, forward plus backward, each architecture as the recipe trains it (ISLA on the fused geometry kernel, GeoTransolver compiled). Memory "
      "is the peak allocated by the step; the step is the median over the timed steps. How to read this: the table states cost, not accuracy (the "
      "standing of these configurations is in @sec-surface); the ratio columns are each architecture ÷ ISLA, above one meaning the architecture "
      "costs more. It does not show Transolver, whose row is in @tbl-cost-200k, nor the eager geometry region, which computes the same function "
      "at about three times the memory (@sec-cost-sweep). "
      "Data: results/cost_sweep_ref_gb300_bf16_2026-09-22.json. {#tbl-isla-cost}")
```

Three practical consequences:

- **Leave `geo_kernel` at its default (`null`).** On CUDA in three
  dimensions with one to four per-point vectors, the model selects the
  fused kernel at the first forward pass and logs the choice. Off CUDA, in
  two dimensions, with rank-2 per-token inputs, or with more than four
  vectors in all, it falls back to the eager recompute region. Force
  `eager` only to reproduce the exact arithmetic path of a checkpoint
  trained on the eager region.
- **On the eager path, leave `geo_checkpoint: true` unless you are short
  of time and long on memory.** It is bitwise identical in outputs and
  gradients. Under the fused kernel the recompute is built in and the flag
  has no effect.
- **Leave `interior_nn_chunk` at its default.** It sizes the blocks of the
  nearest-boundary search's float64 fallback (off CUDA or outside three
  dimensions) and changes cost only; on CUDA in three dimensions the fused
  search ignores it.

## Contracts you can check on your own data {#sec-using-contracts}

**Each contract is a one-line test on a loaded checkpoint, and a residual
far above float32 rounding points at the inputs, not the model.** The
contracts are exact properties of the code (@sec-isla-contracts), and each
is cheap to test on a loaded checkpoint. Rotate and translate the boundary
meshes and the global directions by a random rigid motion, then compare
the scalars (unchanged) and the vectors (rotated). Scale the mesh by $k$,
with the effective measures by $k^2$ (unchanged). Scale the effective
measures alone (unchanged). Split every boundary cell into two coincident
half-measure copies (unchanged: the same measure, re-represented). In
float32 the residuals on the trained checkpoints are at the level of
float32 roundoff. In bf16 autocast they are several percent, mostly
rounding (@sec-isla-contracts). A residual far above these on your own
data points at the inputs, not the model: cells with inconsistent
orientation, effective measures that do not sum to the boundary's measure,
or positions that were centered or scaled by something sample-dependent
before the model saw them. The model normalizes the normals and the global
vectors itself, so their magnitudes cannot cause a residual.
